column5: ذ ك ر (B004/B009); Hebrew זכור, Sabbath memory
column6: The Hebrew imperative zakhor, cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر, makes remembering the Sabbath an act of sanctification; it gives a Torah precedent for remembrance becoming enacted worship.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003/B004); Hebrew זכרון, law in the mouth
column6: Passover is to be a sign and zikkaron so that the Lord's law will be in Israel's mouth, closely joining visible memorial, oral retention, and practice in the manner developed by the commentary.

column5: written tablets given for instruction
column6: God gives Moses tablets, law, and commandment written for Israel's instruction, a direct antecedent for the commentary's link between received revelation, written pages, and later teaching.

column5: ذ ك ر (B004/B009); Hebrew זכרון, trumpet memorial
column6: Trumpet blasts over offerings become a memorial before God; this is a precise ritual and auditory counterpart to the commentary's broad sense of dhikr as worshipful remembrance rather than bare recollection.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003); remembering deliverance through Sabbath practice
column6: Israel is to remember slavery and redemption and therefore keep Sabbath; the verse makes memory of an earlier act the reason for present obedience, as the commentary makes recovered memory lead to prayer and action.

column5: words placed upon the heart
column6: The words commanded by God are to be upon the heart, furnishing an especially close Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary's image of a reminder being held inwardly rather than merely heard.

column5: repeat the words to children in daily speech
column6: The heart-held words are to be repeated to children at home and on the way, an exact domestic form of the commentary's movement from retained revelation to another person's remembrance.

column5: warning not to forget the liberating Lord
column6: Deuteronomy warns Israel not to forget the Lord after entering prosperity; it supplies the ethical danger against which the commentary defines reminder as the opposite of letting something escape the mind.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003/B001); remember God who gives power for wealth
column6: Israel must remember the Lord who gives power to acquire wealth, a cognate-root use that places remembrance beside material benefit and corrects self-sufficient possession in a way relevant to the commentary's test of what truly benefits.

column5: set hearts on the testimony and command children
column6: Moses tells Israel to set its heart on the testimony and command its children to do it, giving a close parallel to the commentary's sequence of inward retention, teaching, and ethical effect.

column5: word is life, not an empty matter
column6: The testimony is not an empty word but Israel's life and the source of long days; this directly supplies a biblical measure of the beneficial word that the commentary seeks in ن ف ع (B001).

column5: book in the mouth, meditation, doing, success
column6: Joshua keeps the Torah book in his mouth and meditates on it continually so as to do it and prosper, closely linking page, recitation, retained thought, action, and beneficial outcome.

column5: ذ ك ر (B004/B007); remembering God's name against worldly power
column6: Against reliance on chariots and horses, the psalmist remembers the name of the Lord; it illuminates the commentary's dhikr as both naming God and a counterweight to reliance on worldly means.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003); wondrous works made memorable
column6: The Lord makes his wonders into a zekher, a memorial; this cognate-root formulation closely supports the commentary's claim that visible divine acts in the world are material for reminder.

column5: never forget precepts that give life
column6: The psalmist will not forget God's precepts because through them God gives life, directly binding anti-forgetfulness to benefit in the way the commentary's conditional reminder does.

column5: do not forget teaching; heart keeps commandments
column6: Proverbs pairs not forgetting instruction with the heart's keeping commandments, a compact wisdom analogue to the commentary's mental preservation of reminder before outward obedience.

column5: teaching written on the tablet of the heart
column6: Instruction is bound on the fingers and written on the tablet of the heart, joining physical inscription with interior retention and sharpening the commentary's pages-and-container imagery.

column5: words kept within and ready on the lips
column6: Wise words are pleasant when kept within and ready on the lips, a direct parallel to the commentary's claim that what is held mentally can become the hearer's own spoken word.

column5: message written on tablet and book for future days
column6: A prophetic charge is fixed on tablet and book for the time to come, offering a precise counterpart to the commentary's concern with preserving a word on pages for readers beyond its first hearing.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003); remember and stand firm
column6: Isaiah calls transgressors to remember and stand firm; this cognate-root imperative supplies a Hebrew prophetic form of the commentary's tadhkirah addressed to those in danger of turning aside.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003/B006); remember former things and confess one God
column6: The command to remember former things leads to the confession that God alone is God, directly linking the commentary's prior-word remembrance with its insistence on the creator over powerless objects.

column5: look to Abraham as ancestral point of instruction
column6: Isaiah directs its hearers to look to Abraham and Sarah as the beginning of a blessed people; it gives a biblical way of making Abraham a remembered source for later communal instruction beside the commentary's Abrahamic sheets.

column5: ذ ك ر (B003); fear, not remembering, and not laying to heart
column6: Isaiah asks whom Israel feared so that it neither remembered God nor laid him to heart, a striking inverse of the commentary's pairing of reverent fear with remembrance held inwardly.

column5: people forget God for days without number
column6: Jeremiah contrasts a bride who remembers clothing with a people that have forgotten God, providing a vivid prophetic parallel to the commentary's account of forgetfulness as abandonment of the very one to be remembered.

column5: Torah written within and on hearts
column6: Jeremiah relocates Torah from external writing to the inward heart; this complements and complicates the commentary's relation between earlier sheets and the listener's internal capacity to hold the reminder.

column5: righteous person warned, takes warning, and lives
column6: When the righteous person receives warning and does not sin, that person lives and the prophet is delivered; this necessary positive counterpart to the watchman scene maps the commentary's reminder when it actually benefits its hearer.

column5: hear prophetic speech but do not do it
column6: Ezekiel's audience listens to the prophet's pleasant song but refuses to do what it says; this gives a concrete biblical instance of hearing without the inward holding and action that the commentary calls beneficial.

column5: forgotten Torah followed by reciprocal forgetting
column6: Hosea says that because the people forgot God's Torah, God will forget their children; it makes the commentary's memory-forgetting contrast into a judicial outcome.

column5: priestly lips guard knowledge; people seek Torah from the mouth
column6: Knowledge is guarded by the priest's lips and sought by the people from that messenger's mouth, a close counterpart to the commentary's teacher who receives and explains a prior word to others.

column5: public Torah reading with explanation for understanding
column6: The Torah is read aloud, explained, and made understood; this exact public-reading scene supplies a Hebrew Bible analogue to the commentary's recitation followed by clarification for its listeners.

column5: study, do, and teach Torah
column6: Ezra sets his heart to study Torah, do it, and teach its statutes; this is a particularly clear threefold pattern for the commentary's received word, personal retention, and subsequent reminder.

column5: city believes warning and changes its practice
column6: Nineveh believes God's warning, fasts, and changes response; the scene shows the conditional benefit of a prophetic reminder becoming visible in a hearer's conduct.

column5: creation's visible goods should disclose their maker
column6: Wisdom faults people who see the good things of creation yet fail to know their maker, a Jewish-Hellenistic counterpart to the commentary's created order as a public reminder that can still be missed.

column5: human-made objects called gods
column6: Wisdom calls those unhappy who place hope in dead, human-made things named gods; it tightly parallels the commentary's Abrahamic examination of whether cult objects can truly help their worshippers.

column5: Moses receives Torah and transmits it through generations
column6: Avot's chain from Moses to Joshua, elders, prophets, and the Great Assembly gives a Jewish traditional model for revelation preserved through successive human reminders.

column5: Moses' staff among twilight-created marvels
column6: By treating Moses' staff as one of the exceptional creations at twilight, Avot recasts the commentary's ordinary, useful staff as a primordial sign; the contrast is itself an instructive later reception of the object.

column5: remember ancestral deeds for honor and lasting name
column6: Mattathias tells his sons to remember the ancestors' deeds so as to receive honor and an everlasting name, directly connecting remembered prior tradition with the commentary's secondary sense of dhikr as renown.

column5: commandments of life and learned wisdom
column6: Baruch calls Israel to hear commandments of life and learn wisdom, a Jewish scriptural articulation of remembered instruction as life-giving benefit rather than mere information.

column5: pay attention to heard things lest they drift away
column6: Hebrews urges greater attention to what was heard so that it does not drift away, an exceptionally close New Testament formulation of the commentary's concern with a received word being lost unless held.

column5: hearer immediately forgets after looking
column6: James depicts the hearer who looks and then immediately forgets; this supplies the concrete negative image behind the commentary's contrast between reminder retained and reminder that passes by.

column5: let what was heard from the beginning abide
column6: The community is told to let the original message abide in it; this directly joins the commentary's prior word to an enduring inner dwelling rather than a momentary hearing.

column5: sayings treasured and pondered in the heart
column6: Mary keeps and ponders the sayings in her heart, a narrative counterpart to the commentary's image of an inward vessel that holds what has been spoken.

column5: hear God's word and keep it
column6: Jesus calls blessed those who hear God's word and keep it, a concise Christian parallel to the commentary's distinction between an offered reminder and beneficial, obedient retention.

column5: disciples remember a saying and believe Scripture
column6: After the resurrection the disciples remember Jesus' saying and believe both Scripture and his word, showing remembrance as a later recovery that makes prior speech intelligible.

column5: reading Scripture followed by explained proclamation
column6: Philip begins from the passage being read and explains its good news, closely matching the commentary's pattern of a received written word being made intelligible to another person.

column5: unceasing personal admonition to remember
column6: Paul tells the elders to remember his three years of unceasing warning; it gives a concrete apostolic example of reminder as sustained pastoral responsibility rather than coercive control.

column5: word of grace builds and gives inheritance
column6: Paul entrusts hearers to the word able to build them up and give an inheritance, an explicit account of a proclaimed word's beneficial result.

column5: former events written as instruction for later readers
column6: Israel's earlier events happened as examples and were written for instruction at the end of the ages, a close Christian parallel to the commentary's former pages and visible history functioning as reminder.

column5: former writings give instruction, endurance, and hope
column6: Paul says everything written beforehand was written for instruction so that readers may have hope, directly supporting the commentary's claim that previous scripture remains a usable word for later hearers.

column5: forgotten exhortation addressed to children
column6: Hebrews reproves readers for forgetting the exhortation that addresses them as children, making a prior scriptural warning itself the object that must be recalled.

column5: word choked by cares, riches, and pleasures
column6: In the thorny soil the heard word is choked by cares, riches, and pleasures and reaches no maturity; this directly supplies a Christian picture of why benefit may fail where the commentary contrasts lasting good with worldly preference.

column5: creation known but not honored or thanked
column6: Although people knew God, they neither honored nor thanked him and became futile in thought; this is the negative continuation of creation as a reminder that the commentary says can be seen yet not retained.

column5: deliberate overlooking of creation and water
column6: The opponents deliberately overlook the creation of earth through and by water through God's word, a striking Christian counterpart to the commentary's water-and-creation reminders that can be ignored.

column5: Noah warned of unseen things, reverent, building an ark
column6: Noah acts in reverent fear after a warning about unseen things and prepares an ark; it joins the commentary's fearful receiver, warning, and flood-water scene in one Christian retelling.

column5: heard words put into practice on rock
column6: The wise builder hears Jesus' words and does them, building on rock; this provides a vivid Christian counterpart to the commentary's demand that retained reminder issue in stable, beneficial action.

column5: Timothy sent to remind communities of apostolic ways
column6: Timothy is sent to remind the Corinthians of Paul's ways as taught everywhere, an unusually exact New Testament instance of a messenger being delegated to perform remembrance for others.

column5: learned, received, heard, seen, then practiced
column6: The Philippians are to practice what they learned, received, heard, and saw; its ordered reception-to-practice sequence closely reflects the commentary's account of reminder becoming the hearer's own deed.

column5: sacred writings able to make wise for salvation
column6: Sacred writings are able to make Timothy wise for salvation, a direct Christian analogue to the commentary's prior sheets as a word whose benefit lies in the good to which it leads.

column5: annual sacrificial remembrance of sins
column6: The sacrifices contain an annual remembrance of sins, a distinct Christian liturgical use of memory that bears on the commentary's discussion of dhikr's ritual as well as mental forms.

column5: honor with lips while heart remains distant
column6: Jesus contrasts lip-honor with a heart far from God; this sharpens the commentary's warning that spoken remembrance is only a later branch if the inward holding of the word is absent.

column5: land drinks rain and yields crop, receiving blessing
column6: Land that drinks repeated rain and bears a useful crop receives blessing; it gives a Christian agrarian analogue to the commentary's water, pasture, and beneficial remainder imagery.

column5: thorns after rain are rejected and burned
column6: Land yielding thorns after the same rain is rejected and ends in burning, a specific contrary image for the commentary's one reminder producing different outcomes in its hearers.

column5: remember the one who speaks God's word and honor that speaker
column6: The Didache tells its hearer to remember day and night the person who speaks God's word and to honor that person; it is an early Christian reception of the teacher-reminder relation developed in the commentary.
